AAAB: Highly rated corporate bonds: loans to companies rated Aaa down to A, the strongest borrowers, with under ten years until they come due. It is a cautious core bond holding, paying a little more than Treasuries of similar length while keeping credit risk low.
ABLG: Leading companies outside the US, chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital in the business, currently heavy in Asian and European chipmakers and chip equipment firms. It is a quality-screened foreign holding, so currency moves and the global chip cycle both shape its returns.
ABOT: Innovative large companies chosen for strong free cash flow relative to the capital invested in the business, currently led by chipmakers, device makers and drug companies. It pairs an innovation theme with a cash-flow quality screen, so it behaves like a growth holding with a financial filter on top.
ABXB: A flexible bond fund built from Treasury funds of different lengths, shifted around as the managers judge where the value sits along the maturity range. Owning only government debt keeps credit risk near zero, so its results hinge almost entirely on interest rate calls.
ACGR: Large US growth companies, actively picked by American Century's managers, currently led by the giant chip, software and internet names. It is a growth holding whose results depend on stock selection, so it rises and falls harder than the broad market when big growth names swing.
ACHP: Asian semiconductor companies: the chipmakers, foundries and equipment firms of Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and their neighbors, the heartland of world chip production. It is a regional, single-industry bet, so it combines the chip cycle's swings with the political and currency risks of Asia.
ACYB: A ladder of autocallable contracts, rolled at staggered times, that pay income while the market behaves and build in a buffer against moderate drops. Autocallables can be called away early and cap gains, so it is a structured, income-first product rather than a simple stock or bond holding.
AIQD: An inverse leveraged bet against artificial intelligence stocks: an exchange-traded note designed to deliver three times the opposite of an AI index's daily move. It resets daily and is built for very short trades, so holding it in a rising or choppy market can grind its value down fast.
AMHI: High income municipal bonds: tax-exempt debt from riskier local projects and authorities, industrial development deals, gas agencies and health and education facilities. The interest is generally free of federal tax, and the higher yield comes from borrowers a cautious muni fund would avoid.
BBBB: BBB-rated corporate bonds: loans to companies on the lowest rung of investment grade, one step above junk status. They pay more interest than higher-rated bonds to make up for the extra risk, so this is the yield-tilted end of a cautious bond portfolio.
CPU: The ten largest semiconductor companies, the designers and manufacturers behind the chips in every computer, phone and data center. Limiting the fund to ten giants makes it a concentrated bet on the chip cycle, so it swings hard when chip demand or AI spending shifts.
CTJL: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks that uses options to buffer the first 30% of losses over its outcome period, in exchange for a cap on gains. This July series resets each year, and the protection works as designed only for investors who hold through the full period.
CTJN: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks that uses options to buffer the first 30% of losses over its outcome period, in exchange for a cap on gains. This June series resets each year, and the protection works as designed only for investors who hold through the full period.
EAFH: Stocks from developed markets outside North America, Europe, Japan and their peers, with half of the currency exposure hedged back into dollars. The partial hedge is the twist: it softens currency swings without removing them, so returns split the difference between hedged and unhedged foreign funds.
EMAG: Three giant emerging-market companies at the center of the artificial intelligence race, the Mag 3 of the fund's name, spanning chips and internet platforms in Asia. Owning just three stocks makes this one of the most concentrated funds anywhere, so single-company news can move it violently.
FIFT: Fifty large US companies picked from the biggest-company index by a quantitative model built with Ned Davis Research, favoring dividend payers. It works as a focused core holding, narrower than owning all 500, so its results depend on the model's picks rather than the whole market.
GCB: Intermediate-term bonds from governments and companies: a blend of Treasury and agency debt with investment-grade corporate bonds in the middle maturity range. It is a classic core bond holding, paying a little more than pure government funds while keeping maturities, and price swings, moderate.
GTOH: Short-term high yield bonds: below-investment-grade corporate debt that comes due soon, chosen by Invesco's managers. Short maturities soften the price swings that long junk bonds suffer, but the borrowers are still the riskier kind, so credit worries can move it more than safer short bond funds.
HF: An absolute return fund that mixes stock funds with positions betting against the market, aiming to make money in up and down markets alike. Its mix of long and short holdings means it can look nothing like a normal stock fund, and it will likely trail badly in strong bull markets.
HOID: Companies building humanoid robots and the parts that make them work, motors, sensors, chips and software for machines shaped like people. Humanoid robots are still more promise than product, so this is a speculative bet on a young industry that swings with demos, deals and headlines.
ICOM: Companies that produce commodities, miners, energy firms and farm businesses, chosen with an income tilt by Tema's managers. It offers raw-materials exposure through stocks rather than futures, so it pays dividends like a stock fund while still rising and falling with commodity prices.
IPB: A trust certificate from a 2003 series: a fixed security that pays interest at the rate in its name and is backed by assets held in a trust. Securities like this trade more like a single bond than a diversified fund, so anyone holding it is exposed to that one structure's terms.
LTB: US Treasury bonds with at least twenty years until they mature, the longest-dated debt of the world's safest borrower. Long bonds pay interest for decades and cushion stock portfolios in panics, but their prices swing the most of any Treasury fund when interest rates move.
MTGG: Growth companies from around the world, with a large share outside the US in foreign markets across Asia, Europe and beyond. It is a growth holding that adds currency moves and foreign market moods to the usual stock swings, so it will not move in step with a US-only fund.
OPTO: Photonics companies, the firms working with light itself: lasers, fiber optics, sensors and optical chips, with swaps and options used to add an income blast. It is a narrow bet on light-based technology, a small and fast-moving field, so it swings far more than a broad tech fund.
PBWN: Industrial companies from outside the US: engineering, electrical equipment and machinery giants of Europe and Japan, with industrials at nearly the whole fund. It fills the industrial corner of a foreign stock portfolio, so it swings with global manufacturing and with currencies other than the dollar.
RNMN: A market neutral fund that pairs long and short positions, with much of the book in SPACs, the blank-check companies holding cash while they hunt for a merger. It aims to earn from deal mechanics and price gaps rather than market direction, a specialist strategy whose returns can look odd next to stocks.
SCIN: Bonds issued outside the US: government and corporate debt from developed markets overseas, in a single Schwab fund. It diversifies a bond portfolio beyond US borrowers, and because the bonds are priced in foreign currencies, exchange rate moves can add to or subtract from the interest earned.
SPXP: The 500 biggest US companies, plus an overlay of derivatives designed to add a little extra exposure on top of the index itself. It works like a core stock holding with a slight amplifier attached, so it edges ahead in rising markets and edges behind in falling ones.
SQBR: A defined-outcome fund on US stocks built around a barrier set 20% below the market's starting level, resetting every quarter. If stocks end the quarter above that line, the fund aims to deliver a set gain; if they fall through it, losses arrive much like owning the market.
SVTN: US Treasury bonds with between seven and ten years until they mature, the heart of the government's own medium-to-long-term debt. It pays a bit more than shorter Treasury funds and swings a bit more when rates move, a middle path between cash-like safety and long bond drama.
THRU: The infrastructure behind commodities: pipelines, storage terminals, ports and processing plants that move oil, gas, metals and grain from ground to market. It is a steadier way to own the raw materials economy than buying the commodities themselves, with income from fees for moving and storing them.
TIPG: A ladder of inflation-protected Treasury bonds arranged to mature in steps toward 2046, paying out distributions along the way. The ladder spreads interest rate risk across years instead of betting on one maturity, and the 2046 end date makes it a tool for a goal about twenty years out.
TNTW: US Treasury bonds with between ten and twenty years until they mature, a long stretch of the government's own debt. Bonds this long pay interest for many years and move a lot when rates change, so this is a bolder Treasury holding than the intermediate funds.
TPAY: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to pay managed distributions targeted at 10% a year, using the index's big US companies as the engine rather than holding the stocks themselves. The payout target is the point of the design, so it behaves more like an income product than a growth fund.
TTTT: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, known as TIPS, whose principal adjusts upward with inflation so payments keep their purchasing power. It is a defensive bond holding built for preserving buying power rather than maximizing income, and its price still moves when interest rates change.
UB: US Treasury bonds across maturities: the full range of the government's own debt, from shorter to longer dated issues, in one fund. It is a plain, low-risk core bond holding meant for interest income and safety, and its price still drifts down when interest rates rise.
USFI: US bonds of many kinds, government, mortgage and corporate, actively shifted by Brandywine's managers as they hunt for value across the bond market. It is a core-style bond holding with an active hand on the mix, so it will not behave exactly like a plain index bond fund.
WSLS: US small companies held two ways at once: a long-only portfolio of small caps, plus a long-short overlay that bets on some and against others. The design aims to squeeze more return from small-company stock picking, and the short side can soften drops but adds its own risks.
XLEM: The energy slice of the S&P 500: oil and gas producers, refiners and pipeline companies among America's biggest corporations. It is a focused bet on fuel prices and energy demand, steadier than small energy funds because it owns only the giants, but still hostage to oil.
XLKM: The technology slice of the S&P 500: software makers, chip companies and computer hardware firms drawn from America's biggest corporations. It is a focused bet on the tech sector, so it swings more than the broad market, and some internet giants are classed in other sectors and sit outside it.
XLPM: The consumer staples slice of the S&P 500: makers and sellers of food, drinks, household goods and personal care products. It is a defensive sector holding that usually falls less in downturns and grows more slowly in booms, the steadier corner of a stock portfolio.
XLYM: The consumer discretionary slice of the S&P 500: retailers, carmakers, restaurants, travel firms and online shopping giants. These companies sell things people want rather than need, so the fund does well when households feel confident and falls harder when spending tightens.
XXQQ: The growth giants of the Nasdaq 100, minus a set of companies the manager excludes on principle, which is the redacted part of the name. What remains is still a tech-heavy growth portfolio, so it swings like one, with a values-based screen layered on top.
XXSP: America's 500 largest companies across every major industry, minus a set of companies the manager excludes on principle, the redacted part of the name. What remains still behaves like a core market holding, moving with the US economy, with a values-based screen layered on top.
